content: Prout's hypothesis was an early 19th-century scientific proposition aimed at explaining the existence of various chemical elements by theorizing about the internal structure of the atom. In 1815 and 1816, the English chemist William Prout published two papers in which he noted that the atomic weights of the elements known at the time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight of hydrogen. Based on this observation, he hypothesized that the hydrogen atom was the fundamental building block of matter, and that the atoms of all other elements were composed of groupings of different numbers of hydrogen atoms. Prout's hypothesis had a significant influence on the field of chemistry throughout the 1820s. However, more precise measurements of atomic weights, such as those conducted by Jöns Jakob Berzelius in 1828 and Edward Turner in 1832, revealed discrepancies that contradicted Prout's hypothesis. For example, the atomic weight of chlorine, which was approximately 35.5 times that of hydrogen, could not be explained by Prout's theory. In response, some scientists proposed an ad hoc modification, suggesting that the fundamental unit was half the mass of a hydrogen atom. When further inconsistencies emerged, others speculated that the basic unit might instead be one-quarter of a hydrogen atom. Although these conjectures were ultimately proven incorrect, they stimulated further research and more accurate measurements of atomic weights, which greatly advanced the field of chemistry. The discrepancies in atomic weights were later understood to result from the existence of isotopes—atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. While it is now known that all elements are formed through the nuclear fusion of hydrogen into heavier elements, modern science recognizes that atoms are composed of both protons (hydrogen nuclei) and neutrons. Neutrons within atomic nuclei can decay into protons through the emission of beta radiation. The modern interpretation of Prout's rule states that the atomic mass of a nucleus, defined by its proton number (P) and neutron number (N), is equal to the sum of the masses of its constituent protons and neutrons, minus the binding energy that holds the nucleus together.
